conbody.p: Digital audio is sound that has been converted into a numerical representation. Understanding a few key concepts will help you make better recordings and edits in .
You do not need to understand all these details to start recording. The default settings in work well for most purposes. Come back to this topic later when you want to fine-tune your recordings.

section.title: Waveforms
section.p: Sound travels through air as a continuous of pressure changes. A microphone converts these pressure changes into an electrical signal. To store this signal digitally, the computer takes thousands of measurements (samples) of the signal's amplitude per second.

section.title: Sample Rate
section.p: The is the number of samples captured per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). Common sample rates include:

ul.li: 44,100 Hz (CD quality) — sufficient for most audio work
96,000 Hz — used in professional music production

section.p: A higher sample rate captures more detail but produces larger files.

section.title: Bit Depth
section.p: determines how precisely each sample's amplitude is recorded. Common bit depths are:

ul.li: 32-bit float — used internally by Audacity for lossless editing

dlentry.dd: The height of a sound wave, corresponding to how loud the sound is. Measured in decibels (dB).
Distortion that occurs when the audio signal exceeds the maximum amplitude the system can represent. Appears as flat-topped waveforms.
Mono audio uses a single channel; stereo uses two channels (left and right) to create a sense of spatial width.
